title: Boys Club

jokes.text: So, we've been called out to this hiking trail because there's some reports that some teenagers are digging bags of dog poop out of the trash and having dog poop fights. I don't believe it.
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a bureaucratic, matter-of-fact report about teenagers having dog poop fights
jokes.punchline: 'I don't believe it.' — the mundane skepticism against an obviously disgusting premise
jokes.explanation: The deadpan disbelief at an objectively real and gross scenario is a solid cold-open joke. Leslie's earnest official framing ('I don't believe it') against dog poop warfare is a classic Parks setup — her bureaucratic optimism colliding with absurd reality. Functional and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No way. You're making that up. Teenagers don't have dog poop fights.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God, they're doing it. They're actually doing it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Nope, nope, nope. I'm out of here.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. It's real. Uh... Yeah, I'm not gonna go deal with this. I'm leaving.
jokes.setup: Leslie has called Tom out to help deal with teenagers having dog poop fights
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately announces he's leaving rather than engage
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Tom — no heroics, pure self-preservation. The economy is excellent: he sees the situation, confirms it's real, and immediately bails. His acknowledgment makes it funnier than if he just ran. Strong character integration because this is quintessential Tom Haverford selfishness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone stop! This is not productive! We need to have a calm, rational discussion about—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this is amazing!

jokes.text: Leslie gets hit with dog poop / joins in the dog poop fight — 'Actually, this is a little fun. This is fun.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is horrified by the dog poop fight and is trying to stop it; she gets hit and cries for help
jokes.punchline: She ends up participating and admits she's having fun
jokes.explanation: The arc from horrified bureaucrat to enthusiastic participant in a dog poop fight is a perfect encapsulation of Leslie's character — she fully commits to whatever she's doing. The admission 'this is a little fun' is a great character beat, and physically seeing this happen is where the real comedy lives. Strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And if someone found out I was watching porn, they'd use it against me. Like, 'Leslie Knope watches porn!' And I'd have to explain, 'Well, yes, but only ethical, feminist porn where the women are respected and fairly compensated.' And they'd be like, 'She watches porn!' And I'd be like, 'Yes, but—' And they'd already left.

jokes.text: I love Great Lakes wine. You can have the wine. I want to take that cheese and do terrible things to it.
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie discover a gift basket from Norton Construction with wine and cheese
jokes.punchline: 'I want to take that cheese and do terrible things to it' — the escalating enthusiasm is absurdly sensual
jokes.explanation: Tom's over-the-top foodie sensuality about cheese is a great character moment with strong quotability. The escalation from 'I love Great Lakes wine' to wanting to do 'terrible things' to the cheese subverts expectations nicely. Very Tom — he gives away the wine to fixate on something more specific and absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I rented it from Blockbuster like five times. I wore out the DVD.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, why did I just tell you that?

jokes.text: That's why I go two towns over if I want to rent a movie with nudity in it. Yeah, I probably shouldn't have said that.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining the ethics rules about gifts and says 'we live in a fish bowl and the public is always watching'
jokes.punchline: She reveals she goes two towns over to rent adult movies, immediately recognizes the overshare
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Leslie's extreme rule-following is perfectly illustrated by the absurd logic: she follows ethics so strictly that she drives towns away just to rent a movie with nudity in it (not even explicit porn — 'nudity'). The immediate self-aware 'I probably shouldn't have said that' is the perfect button. It's original, character-specific, well-structured, and deeply quotable. Could only come from Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I would never exploit my government position. That's not who I am. I'm like Superman - I have all this power, but I use it for good.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Now, if you'll excuse me, I need to use the Parks Department's printing equipment to make business cards for my entertainment company.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'Official Parks and Rec business. Just need to grab a quick hot dog. Sorry about that, little girl, you can have the next one.' followed by 'I have a moral code, and I never violate it.'
jokes.setup: Tom opens his talking head claiming he never exploits his power as a government official
jokes.punchline: Cut to him using his government badge to cut in line for a hot dog, pushing ahead of a child
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary irony structure: character declares their virtue, immediately shown violating it. What elevates this above the obvious is the specific detail — he cuts a LITTLE GIRL in line using his government badge for a HOT DOG. The smallness of the crime and the politeness to the child ('you can have the next one') makes it funnier than a grander corruption example would be.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wow, Mark really knows how to pick them. Look at all these beautiful women.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, they're all exactly the same type.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. It's like he has a very specific genetic preference, like he's only attracted to women with identical fake breasts.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's not genetic, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, maybe his great-grandfather was attacked by a woman with real breasts and now it's passed down through the family.

jokes.text: 'You are so pure, you're like a brown Superman with a beard that just stands for justice and truth and the American way.'
jokes.setup: Tom is describing how people perceive his moral purity
jokes.punchline: The self-aggrandizing description is so specific and absurd — 'brown Superman with a beard' — that it circles back to self-parody
jokes.explanation: Tom's self-mythology is a recurring comedic engine. The specificity of 'brown Superman with a beard' is genuinely funny — it's so particular and Tom-specific. The joke slightly overstays its welcome with the full Superman tagline recitation, which costs it some economy points.

jokes.text: April has created a social media profile for a construction pit. The pit already has six friends.
jokes.setup: Leslie asked April to make a social network profile for the Sullivan Street pit (a literal hole in the ground) to raise awareness
jokes.punchline: The pit already has six friends, treated as a legitimate success metric
jokes.explanation: A solid absurdist premise — a hole in the ground has a social media presence with friends. The earnestness with which Leslie treats this as genuine progress is very on-brand for Season 1 Parks. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, Mark, I have to ask you about this. Your favorite movie is 'Battlefield Earth'?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Yeah, so?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So? Mark, that's one of the worst movies ever made. It's scientifically worse than murder.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I like it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm going to have to reject you based on this alone.

jokes.text: Mark's profile photo wall includes women with fake boobs and a woman with a thong on her face; 'Maybe those are his relatives.' 'Yeah, maybe fake boobs run in his family.'
jokes.setup: The group is looking at Mark's social media profile; Ann notes the photos of women
jokes.punchline: Leslie tries to defend Mark ('maybe relatives'), Ann escalates with 'fake boobs run in his family'
jokes.explanation: The setup/payoff structure works well: Leslie's naive defense is immediately skewered by Ann's specific callback to the 'fake boobs' detail. Good comedic escalation within two lines. Ann's 'fake boobs run in his family' is the sharper line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I feel like I'm being watched by all these portraits of dead white men. It's like their eyes are following me everywhere I go.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, that one's definitely looking at my chest.

jokes.text: Mark's favorite movie is Dances With Wolves.
jokes.setup: The group is roasting Mark's social media profile — women with thongs on faces, etc.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, my God, his favorite movie is Dances With Wolves.' — delivered as the most damning revelation
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of escalation and misdirection — after thongs on faces and fake boobs, the crowning horror is an earnest Kevin Costner movie choice. The specificity of Dances With Wolves (not a bad movie, but extremely revealing about a certain type of dudebro) is sharp cultural observation delivered with great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My wife bought me a shirt. She said it makes me look thinner.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't need to look thinner. I need to look exactly like this.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head in front of the wall of city council portraits: 'No matter what direction I move, he's always staring at my chest.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains every day as a woman she walks past a wall of male politicians from the past 30 years, which can be very upsetting — 'especially because of that guy'
jokes.punchline: She moves around and a specific portrait's eyes appear to follow her chest; she demonstrates the effect
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed visual gag that also makes a pointed comment about institutional sexism. The physical demonstration ('See?') elevates it beyond the dialogue alone. Leslie's earnest indignation about a painting staring at her chest perfectly balances the feminist subtext with absurdism. Strong rewatch value because the visual payoff is key.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I could use a beer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann! A woman, drinking a beer? That's so brave. You're like the Rosa Parks of having a drink that isn't a cosmopolitan.

jokes.text: Sure, yeah. I could use a beer. / 'Yes, Ann! That's good, think like a man.'
jokes.setup: Leslie rallies Ann to go bust up the boys' club, framing it in high-minded feminist terms
jokes.punchline: Ann's motivation is purely 'I could use a beer'; Leslie congratulates her for 'thinking like a man'
jokes.explanation: The gap between Leslie's idealistic framing and Ann's practical desire for beer is a good comedic beat. Leslie inadvertently undermining her own feminist argument by praising Ann for 'thinking like a man' is the sharp ironic punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I'm putting you in charge of this project.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because you're a strong, independent woman who doesn't need a man to tell you what to do. Girl power!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm in charge because I'm competent, not because of my gender.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right, yes, of course. But also, you're a woman doing it, so that's amazing.

jokes.text: April tells Leslie she's 'in charge' 'because you're a woman!'
jokes.setup: Leslie leaves April in charge as she heads out to infiltrate the boys' club
jokes.punchline: April deadpans 'What, do you really like red tape and uphill battles?' — clarifying she sees being put in charge as a burden due to Leslie's feminist overcompensation
jokes.explanation: April's nihilistic deflation of Leslie's enthusiasm is in character, and the 'do you really like red tape and uphill battles?' line shows April's characteristic cynicism about Leslie's idealism. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're here to join your club.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This isn't a club. We just drink beer and talk.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly. A club. With initiation ceremonies, secret handshakes, and a strict code of conduct that binds us together in eternal brotherhood.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: There's no code of conduct.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not yet.

jokes.text: Leslie storms up to bust up the 'boys' club' — it turns out to be two guys casually drinking beers in a courtyard. 'Awesome. Glad to have you. Let me get you a beer.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has built up the 'boys' club' as an exclusive, powerful institution that she needs to 'bust up'
jokes.punchline: It's just a couple of guys having casual beers outside; they immediately and warmly welcome her
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Leslie's grand feminist mission is executed perfectly — all her ideological preparation hits a brick wall of cheerful normalcy. The contrast between her 'we're busting up your little boys' club' and the immediate 'awesome, glad to have you' is sharp and efficient. Also seeds the real theme of the episode: the barrier was in Leslie's head.

jokes.text: 'Did you hear that? That was the sound of a glass ceiling being shattered.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been immediately welcomed into the boys' club hangout without any resistance
jokes.punchline: She interprets this total non-event as a historic feminist triumph
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Leslie mishears or misreads a completely ordinary social moment as a landmark achievement. The structure is perfect — the 'sound of a glass ceiling being shattered' is a talking-head moment that reframes the mundane warmth she just experienced as a historic victory. Highly quotable, perfectly in character, and the economy is exceptional. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Mark has this friend on Facebook who spells 'lose' as 'loose' and 'your' as 'you're' in every single post.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: The double misspelling makes it even more ridiculous.

jokes.text: Tom's talking head: 'I kind of feel like I'm already in the boys' club. I mean, look at those bitches clean up after me.'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining his relationship to the boys' club concept
jokes.punchline: He reveals he's referring to women in general cleaning up after him — an oblivious sexism that also indicts him
jokes.explanation: Tom's oblivious sexism is in character, but this joke is the weakest form of it — the word choice makes it more crude than clever. The joke works as character revelation but doesn't have the wit of Tom's better moments. It's a cheap shortcut compared to other Tom lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay. Mark, that was weak. You're going to have to do better than that. Here, let me show you how it's done.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You see, a good comeback needs structure, timing, and confidence. You just sort of... mumbled something about her being... I don't even know what you were going for.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Let's try again. Ann says something mean, and you respond with something that's clever, but not mean-spirited. It's about the delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come on, Mark. I know you can do better. I believe in you.

jokes.text: Ann teases Mark about the girls with 'tribal back tattoos who drink Red Bull for a living.' 'Oh! Oh, I like this. This is banter. Banter's fun.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks Mark about his social scene; she and Leslie have been looking at his profile's female friends
jokes.punchline: The specific 'tribal back tattoos who drink Red Bull for a living' is a very precise cultural type; Mark's enthusiastic recognition of 'banter' suggests he's delighted and slightly starved for wit
jokes.explanation: The cultural specificity of 'tribal back tattoos who drink Red Bull for a living' is sharp observational comedy, and Mark's genuine delight at 'banter' adds a layer of character comedy. Two good jokes stacked: the insult and then Mark's almost child-like excitement about being sparred with.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Hey, it's April. Yeah, I need you to do something for me. No, I'm not asking. If you don't, I'm going to come to your house and bedazzle all your jeans. Every single pair. With a hot glue gun.

jokes.text: You know, you have a friend who has a tattoo that says 'Daddy's Girl.' And both words are misspelled.
jokes.setup: Ann and Leslie have been looking at Mark's profile; they bring up his friends as ammunition for banter
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'Daddy's Girl' (already amusing) to 'both words are misspelled' is the payoff
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's tightest jokes. 'Both words are misspelled' is a perfect button — the audience is already smiling at the tattoo concept, then the escalation lands hard. Great economy, excellent structure. The mispelling of both four-letter words in a tattoo is a very specific and funny image.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: A party without beer is just people standing in a room. Which is what we were doing at the DMV yesterday.

jokes.text: Mark's comeback to the roasting: 'Those aren't really my friends anymore. I don't hang out with them.' 'Boo. Brendanawicz, that's some weak sauce. You need to hit harder!'
jokes.setup: Leslie/Ann have been roasting Mark about his social media friends; Mark is expected to fire back
jokes.punchline: His 'comeback' is a pathetic retreat; Tom calls him out for it
jokes.explanation: Mark's deflation works both as character comedy (he's revealed to be somewhat ashamed of his social circle) and as a comedic beat where the expected comeback doesn't come. Tom's 'weak sauce' commentary is the sharper line. Together they form a good exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I may have opened the gift basket from the Sweetums people before I was supposed to. And I feel terrible about it. Like, genuinely terrible. I mean, I know it's just a gift basket, but I violated the sacred trust between a public servant and a corporation that's trying to influence her decisions. I'm a horrible person. I'm corrupt. I'm basically a supervillain now.

jokes.text: April on the phone: 'Natalie, it's your sister. Pick me up or I'm gonna draw all over your jeans.'
jokes.setup: April is left alone in the Parks office, waiting for a ride
jokes.punchline: Her threat is oddly specific, petty, and perfectly teenage — 'draw all over your jeans'
jokes.explanation: This is a gem of a line. April's threat is so specific and childish (drawing on jeans, not even burning them or anything dramatic) that it reveals her whole personality in one line. It's excellent character integration — the threat fits perfectly in the absurd space between teenager and deadpan weirdo that makes April funny. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've decided to apologize to every female politician in America. Alphabetically. It's the only way to be fair and thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's... that's thousands of people.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm aware, Ben. I've already started. I'm on my third letter. 'Dear Congresswoman Abernathy, I'm sorry for not believing in you hard enough. Your hair looked nice in that one photo from 2003.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're apologizing to them about their hair?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm being personal. That's what makes it meaningful. 'Dear Senator Caldwell, I regret every negative thought I've ever had about your voting record. Also, your shoes are really professional.'

jokes.text: The party breaking up because they ran out of beer — 'Uh, yeah, 'cause parties usually get started when you run out of booze.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to keep the good feeling going as people start to leave after the beer runs out
jokes.punchline: Mark's dry observation that parties don't start when booze runs out
jokes.explanation: A competent deadpan line that punctures Leslie's enthusiasm. Not particularly original — it's an obvious truth stated drily — but it serves its function in the scene and is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann is amazing. She's smart, she's beautiful, she's got a great sense of humor. Honestly, I would say that she's one of the hardest working people I know.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hard... workers.

jokes.text: Leslie bursts in with the contraband gift basket: 'I got wine! / And cheese!' — crowd cheers
jokes.setup: The gift basket was locked up as contraband due to ethics rules; Leslie has been positioned as the strict rule-follower
jokes.punchline: She produces the stolen basket to save the party, completely abandoning her principles for social acceptance
jokes.explanation: The callback to the forbidden basket pays off the earlier setup well. The irony of the ultra-ethical Leslie stealing contraband for social acceptance into a 'boys' club' is the episode's core joke made manifest. The triumphant cheese/wine announcement against the crowd cheering is a good escalation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna clean this house for Ann. You know what? I'm gonna do it right now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what would make this easier? If I do some cocaine.

jokes.text: Leslie's morning-after talking head confession: 'Last night, in a foolish attempt to infiltrate a boys' club, I violated the government employee ethics code of the state of Indiana.'
jokes.setup: We cut from Leslie's triumph with the wine basket to the next morning
jokes.punchline: The gravity of her confession language — 'foolish attempt,' 'violated the ethics code' — applied to opening a gift basket
jokes.explanation: Leslie's disproportionate self-flagellation is a core character trait played well here. Treating opening a gift basket as an ethics code violation worthy of a formal statement is a great character beat. The specific legal language about 'the state of Indiana' adds to the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're breaking the rules? You? Leslie Knope is breaking the rules? I feel like I'm in the Twilight Zone right now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is my thing! I break the rules, you follow them perfectly, and you judge me for it. That's our whole dynamic!

jokes.text: Leslie's apology to female politicians in alphabetical order, starting with Michele Bachmann: 'Michele Bachmann, Republican, Minnesota. I am sorry.' / 'Tammy Baldwin, Democrat, Wisconsin. I'm so sorry, Tammy.' / 'Melissa Bean.' [long pause]
jokes.setup: Leslie says she'd like to apologize to every female public official in America 'individually, and in alphabetical order'
jokes.punchline: She actually starts doing it — with full political party and state affiliations — and the joke escalates as she reaches Melissa Bean and apparently continues at length
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The setup ('individually, and in alphabetical order') is already funny as a Leslie-specific excessive commitment to process. Then she ACTUALLY DOES IT — with party affiliation and state — and the sequence ending on 'Melissa Bean' with a silent cut is perfectly structured. It shows Leslie's earnestness turning into comedy through sheer commitment. Deeply character-specific, well-structured, and earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You wrote me up for calling my mom during work hours.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You were using government time for personal calls.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, my mom was in the hospital. She had emergency surgery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, you should have requested time off like everyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My mother was dying!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Dying or not, there are procedures. I don't make the rules.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You literally do make the rules. You're the deputy director.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly. And as deputy director, I have to set an example.

jokes.text: Andy's living situation revealed: 'Good morning.' / 'Double shift, remember? So I won't see you till tomorrow.' / 'I got dinner. Oh, God. Honey, can you just clean up a little bit?' / 'I'll try. Don't expect much.'
jokes.setup: Ann is heading out for a double shift as a nurse; we get a glimpse of the state of their home
jokes.punchline: Andy's cheerful helplessness ('Don't expect much') and the implied disaster of the apartment
jokes.explanation: The Andy/Ann domestic situation is a slow-burn character setup. 'Don't expect much' is a good understated line that establishes Andy's cheerful incompetence. The visual of the messy apartment is where the real comedy lives. Functional setup scene more than a standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I really need your support on this.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Have you considered prison? It might give you time to think about what you've done.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'She is an angel. And I seriously love her. Hard.'
jokes.setup: Andy is gushing about Ann's saintliness in caring for him
jokes.punchline: 'Hard.' — delivered as a single-word intensifier after a pause, which is both earnest and absurd
jokes.explanation: The pause and then 'Hard.' as the button is a brilliant piece of comedy economy. The word carries multiple readings simultaneously (genuine intensity, inadvertent double-entendre), and the fact that it's clearly sincere makes it even funnier. Chris Pratt's delivery is implied by the transcript structure. Economy score nearly perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This isn't a big deal for Mark. He's used to not having privileges. I mean, look at him. He dresses like a 1970s pornographer. And we're not even going to talk about that mustache. Actually, we are going to talk about that mustache. We're going to include the mustache as a privilege category.

jokes.text: Andy's list for cleaning while Ann is gone; 'I took a bunch of painkillers. They're about to kick in so I'm ready to go.'
jokes.setup: Andy has two broken legs; he's made a list of cleaning tasks to complete while Ann is on her double shift
jokes.punchline: He's prepared for this domestic effort by taking 'a bunch of painkillers,' treating them as a performance enhancer for cleaning
jokes.explanation: This is darkly funny — Andy treating prescription painkillers as a cleaning performance enhancer. The obliviousness about his own predicament is very Andy, and 'they're about to kick in so I'm ready to go' has the cheerful energy of someone talking about pre-workout, not opioids. Good dark subversive comedy that stays funny rather than bleak.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You know, the cover-up is always worse than the crime. It's like when you get mud on your white pants, and then you try to clean it with more mud. Now you're double dirty.

jokes.text: Tom to Leslie: 'Really. Leslie Knope. Usually such a prudish stickler for the rules.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is confessing to opening the gift basket; Tom is playing the scandalized observer
jokes.punchline: Tom's theatrical shock at Leslie's minor transgression, using 'prudish stickler' as if she's committed a felony
jokes.explanation: Tom enjoying Leslie's downfall is funny but this particular line is fairly generic. 'Prudish stickler' isn't a fresh enough observation. Functional character interaction but not a standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm a nester. I like to build a comfortable home for myself.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's just that my nest happens to look like a tornado hit a dumpster.

jokes.text: Tom wrote Leslie up for making personal calls. 'Yes, I did. And I would do it again.' / 'Two wrongs do not make a right.' / 'Yes, but she was in the hospital.' / 'I did not know that at the time.'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to argue that since Leslie wrote him up for calling his hospitalized mother, his basket-taking should be forgiven
jokes.punchline: Leslie's unyielding 'I did not know that at the time' doubles down on her rule-following even in retrospect, with no remorse
jokes.explanation: Leslie's refusal to acknowledge that ignorance about the hospitalization makes her look bad — doubling down with no softening — is excellent character comedy. The callback to the phone call incident works well, and 'I did not know that at the time' delivered without apology is very Leslie. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna get drunk tonight, but like, as a scientist. I'm gonna document everything. How many beers until I can't feel my face? How many until I start crying? How many until I try to fight someone? It's research.

jokes.text: Tom asks for the basket; Leslie refuses saying it's 'evidence.' 'It's a nice basket.' 'What would you put in there?' 'I don't know. Potpourri?' 'That's a lot of potpourri.'
jokes.setup: Tom wants the gift basket; Leslie has refused because it's 'evidence'
jokes.punchline: They drift into a sincere discussion of what to fill the empty basket with; Tom's 'That's a lot of potpourri' is unexpectedly sensible
jokes.explanation: The absurd sincerity of their basket-filling discussion in the middle of an ethics crisis is charming. 'That's a lot of potpourri' is a good understated practical observation that deflates the conversation amusingly. The comedy is in the mundane tangent, very Parks and Rec in tone.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I posted it because I looked really good in that video. My hair was perfect. I don't care about the scandal or the consequences — I just wanted people to see how shiny it was.

jokes.text: 'I appreciate and thank you in advance for your unwavering support.' / 'I think you should go to jail.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is presuming Tom's support as she faces her ethics committee hearing
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately and cheerfully says she should go to jail
jokes.explanation: The setup/punchline structure is clean and the timing works perfectly. Leslie's formal 'I thank you in advance for your unwavering support' vs. Tom's instant 'I think you should go to jail' is a great comedic beat — the gap between her expectation and his response is the joke. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe this is happening. My career is over. Everything I've worked for is gone.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're going to be fine, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How can you say that? Did you see what they're saying about me online?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't go online. It's a cesspool.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm in the cesspool, Ron. I'm drowning in it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Sit down.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm trying, but your bench is incredibly uncomfortable. Why is it so hard?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's walnut. I like it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Of course you do.

jokes.text: 'You're a white Protestant man with a full, rich mustache.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is arguing with Ron that she has to hold herself to a higher standard because of who she is
jokes.punchline: The description of Ron as a 'white Protestant man with a full, rich mustache' — the mustache is listed as a privilege alongside race and religion
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'A full, rich mustache' listed as a form of privilege alongside whiteness and Protestantism is absurdly funny and also weirdly accurate for Ron Swanson. The line works on multiple levels: it's a genuine observation about institutional advantage, it's character-specific (Ron's mustache is famously magnificent), and the escalation from race/religion to the mustache is a perfect comedic left turn. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value. Earns 8.5.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have zero drinks per week.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not true. I've seen you drink at least three margaritas a week.

jokes.text: Ron's metaphor for covering up: 'When you spill something and you try to wipe it up with something that's dirty, then you get double dirty.'
jokes.setup: Ron says 'the cover-up is worse than the crime'; Leslie pushes back for clarification
jokes.punchline: His explanation of the metaphor is so literal and simple that it deflates the Watergate reference to kindergarten wisdom
jokes.explanation: Ron's matter-of-fact deconstruction of his own maxim into a cleaning metaphor is very him — he's wise, but in the most literal, physical terms. The juxtaposition of Watergate-level gravitas ('the cover-up is worse than the crime') reduced to 'double dirty' is the joke. Works on the character level and structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a question for you. In all the years you've known me, have you ever known me to be a liar?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Tom, you're one of the most honest people I know.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so when I tell you that I definitely have a six-pack under this shirt, you believe me?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, no. No, that's not true. You're a liar.

jokes.text: Leslie announces she's e-mailing a full confession to 'everyone in the entire Pawnee government' and has attached a link to the pit's web page 'just to remind people of all the good work that I do.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is taking extraordinary steps to make amends for opening the basket
jokes.punchline: She cannot help but slip a self-promotional link into her confession e-mail
jokes.explanation: The self-promotional impulse breaking through Leslie's sincere self-flagellation is perfect character comedy. She can't confess without also reminding everyone of her good work. The addition of the pit website link to the mass confession e-mail is a great comedic detail — petty, self-serving, and completely Leslie. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So like, what if we were both in a hot air balloon, but it was filled with chocolate pudding instead of air, and we had to use our bodies to propel it upward?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Or what if you were a sentient piece of sushi and I was a very polite diner, but also a merman?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, what if we were both clouds, but sexy clouds, and we could only communicate through interpretive dance and the smell of burnt toast?

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'I wish I could say some of this mess was Ann's, but it's all mine. I'm kind of a nester.'
jokes.setup: We see the disastrous state of Andy's apartment while Ann is on shift
jokes.punchline: 'I'm kind of a nester' — applying a cozy domestic term to what is clearly a disaster zone
jokes.explanation: Andy's self-description as a 'nester' for what is clearly a pigsty is a lovely piece of character self-deception. The word 'nester' has such specific warm-cozy connotations that applying it to filth is a good misdirection. Also the honest admission 'none of this mess is Ann's' is an endearing Andy moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I can't shower with these casts on, so I've been using this dog-washing method on myself.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's disgusting.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, but it works! I just stand in the backyard with the hose.

jokes.text: 'Huh? Not bad for a guy with two broken legs.'
jokes.setup: Andy has apparently accomplished something domestic despite having two broken legs
jokes.punchline: His proud self-assessment is undercut by the implied visual of what 'not bad' looks like in his condition
jokes.explanation: The low bar of pride — 'not bad for a guy with two broken legs' — is endearingly Andy. His pride in whatever small thing he's done despite being literally disabled is sweet and funny. The visual of a hobbled man doing minor domestic tasks is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You stole my boom box? That's not cool, man.

dialogue.speaker: Neighbor
dialogue.line: Yeah, I did. What are you gonna do about it?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, first of all, those are some really expensive batteries in there. Do you have any idea how much I spent on those? You better be taking good care of them.

jokes.text: April: 'I'm doing a little experiment tonight to see what will get me drunker. Drinking wine... / Right now, drinking wine is winning...'
jokes.setup: Leslie discovers that April has been drinking the stolen wine in the office
jokes.punchline: April has framed getting drunk as a scientific experiment and is narrating the ongoing results
jokes.explanation: April framing underage drinking as a scientific experiment is very on-brand for her character — the clinical detachment applied to something she's clearly just doing for fun. 'Right now, drinking wine is winning' as an ongoing experimental update is a great line. Excellent character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is a witch hunt. A witch hunt of the highest order. You're treating Leslie Knope like she's a terrorist, when all she did was throw a small party in a public park.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You know what this reminds me of? The Spanish Inquisition. Pure persecution.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Actually, this is worse than the Spanish Inquisition. This is the Salem witch trials combined with the Holocaust.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No, wait. This is worse than all of human history combined. Future generations will look back on this moment as the darkest day in the history of mankind.

jokes.text: April explains why she posted the video: 'Because I was waiting for my sister and I was bored, and my hair looked really good.'
jokes.setup: Leslie demands to know why April posted a video of Leslie drinking the stolen wine on the pit's website
jokes.punchline: April's reasons: boredom, waiting, and — crucially — her hair looking really good
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best lines. The escalation of mundane justifications ('bored,' 'waiting for my sister') that concludes with 'my hair looked really good' as if that's a perfectly sufficient reason to sabotage your boss is quintessential April Ludgate. The hair reason is so specific and so teenager-brained that it perfectly captures her character. High quotability, strong rewatch value. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't defend Leslie because I like her. I defend her because I hate bureaucracy. My ideal government is a dystopian sexual fantasy.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I just sent an e-mail to everyone in the government, and I put a link to this page!'
jokes.setup: Leslie previously sent a mass confession e-mail and included a link to the pit's website to showcase her good work
jokes.punchline: The pit's website now has video evidence of Leslie drinking stolen wine — her own self-promotional link has condemned her
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Leslie's self-promotional confession e-mail is beautifully constructed. Her attempt to remind people of her good work has instead broadcast evidence of her crime to all of government. This is excellent structural comedy — two separate setups (the mass e-mail and April's video) collide into a single devastating punchline. Strong earned payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I did everything to impress Mark. I got my hair cut, I wore heels, I even learned about sports. I watched the entire 2004 World Series.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: That was eight years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Jerry (unnamed, background character) gleefully replays the video for everyone: 'Play it again for us, Jerry.' / 'You got it.'
jokes.setup: The video of Leslie drinking stolen wine is playing in the office
jokes.punchline: Jerry's eager compliance in replaying Leslie's humiliation is a small but good character beat
jokes.explanation: A brief character beat — Jerry's pathetic enthusiasm to replay Leslie's downfall. Functional as a small character establishing joke but nothing exceptional. The 'You got it' has decent timing.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm not one to judge Leslie's dating choices, but at least Mark has a job. Andy once thought a stop sign was a suggestion.

jokes.text: Caption on April's video: 'A young law-breaker. A future Leslie Knope.'
jokes.setup: The video April posted shows her drinking the wine and has a caption she added
jokes.punchline: April has already memorialized herself as 'a future Leslie Knope' — connecting Leslie's ambition to April's mischief via the shared crime
jokes.explanation: April captioning herself as 'a future Leslie Knope' while committing a crime is sharp and layered — it ironically connects the two characters' rebellious moments while also teasing the genuine mentor/mentee relationship they'll develop. Clever, economical, and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What happened to your scratches?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A jagweed attacked me.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What's a jagweed?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's like a regular weed, but it's a jag.

jokes.text: Leslie panics on the uncomfortable bench in Ron's office: 'This bench is so uncomfortable. Ow. Help. Please, Ron. Ron.' / 'Ron? Where are you?' / 'It's... It'll... Hang in.' / Ron disappears
jokes.setup: Leslie is in crisis about possibly getting fired; she's looking to Ron for emotional support
jokes.punchline: Her distress gets sidetracked by the bench being uncomfortable; Ron's response is useless reassurance followed by quietly disappearing
jokes.explanation: Ron's emotional unavailability is a good character beat — he gives vague encouragement and then simply ceases to be there. Leslie's physical complaint about the bench intruding into her emotional crisis is charming. Not the sharpest joke but a good character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I cleaned the whole house. I'm thinking tonight we're gonna have some amazing sex.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Andy!

jokes.text: Tom's mock deposition: 'How many drinks do you have per week, on average?' / 'Zero.' / 'Zero to six.' / 'I'm gonna write down 10.'
jokes.setup: Tom is running mock deposition questions to prep Leslie for the hearing
jokes.punchline: Tom ignores Leslie's answer entirely and simply escalates the number she gave — 'zero' becomes 'zero to six' becomes 'I'm gonna write down 10'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 0 to 'zero to six' to 'I'll write down 10' is a well-structured three-beat joke. Tom's oblivious/corrupt record-keeping against Leslie's honest protest is a good comedic dynamic. The structure is tight and the escalation pays off well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mark, I'm worried about that letter in my file. It could ruin everything.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Leslie, everyone breaks rules. It's not a big deal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you mean everyone breaks rules?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I mean, Ben parks in handicapped spots, Jerry files things wrong on purpose, and Tom... well, Tom breaks pretty much every rule that exists.

jokes.text: Tom's deposition question: 'Have you ever thought about Ron sexually? Including dreams.' / 'Have you ever had a sexual dream about our boss, Ron Swanson?' / 'No! Absolutely not. No. Yes. No.'
jokes.setup: Tom's mock deposition has devolved into absurd personal questions
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response to 'have you had a sexual dream about Ron?' falls apart into 'No! Absolutely not. No. Yes. No.' — the 'Yes' slipping out is the payoff
jokes.explanation: The accidental 'Yes' slipping out in the middle of Leslie's denial is a classic comedy technique executed well. The rapid-fire 'No! Absolutely not. No. Yes. No.' where the 'Yes' is clearly involuntary is very funny and says a lot about Leslie's relationship with authority figures. Well-structured, character-specific, and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm in the boys' club! I'm in the boys' club! I'm in the boys' club!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you can stop now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm in the boys' club! I'm in the boys' club! I'm in the boys' club!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, that's getting weird.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm in the boys' club. I'm in the boys' club. I'm in the boys' club.

jokes.text: Tom's elaborate Ron sexual dream scenario: 'is he half-Ron, half-animal, like a centaur?' / 'Is he wearing a football uniform?' / 'Are you making love to him on a couch shaped like his mustache?' / 'Is he covered in Powerade?'
jokes.setup: Tom has established that Leslie may have had a dream about Ron; now he's elaborating with increasingly specific scenarios
jokes.punchline: The escalation of specificity — centaur, football uniform, mustache couch, Powerade — each detail stranger and funnier than the last
jokes.explanation: The absurdist escalation of Ron Swanson sexual dream scenarios is one of the episode's funniest extended bits. Each image is funnier than the last: the centaur uses Ron's animalistic quality; the mustache couch is genius for its specificity; 'covered in Powerade' is delightfully random. The structure builds well. This is strong absurdist comedy that stays rooted in character — all details are Ron-specific.

jokes.text: 'How about some stolen wine?' — Tom, when Leslie says she needs something to drink during the mock hearing
jokes.setup: Leslie is stressed and says she needs something to drink
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately references the stolen wine — the source of all her current problems
jokes.explanation: Clean callback joke with perfect economy. The entire episode's plot compressed into two words. Tom's timing here is ideal.

jokes.text: Tom concludes the mock deposition: 'Thank you for your time, Miss Knope. You're fired.' / 'So, that's kind of your worst-case scenario, you know? If you can handle that, I think you'll be fine.'
jokes.setup: Tom has run a chaotic mock deposition that went completely off the rails with Ron dream questions
jokes.punchline: He wraps it up formally with 'you're fired' and then reassures her that was the worst case and she'll be fine — as if that deposition was realistic prep
jokes.explanation: A good button on the deposition scene. Tom's cheerful 'you'll be fine' after that disaster of a prep session is funny because it's delivered with complete sincerity. Functional capper to a strong extended scene.

jokes.text: Andy's washing scene: 'There's only one more thing I need to clean, me. / Um, I can't really get into a shower, so I got this idea from my parents. / This is how they clean their dog.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been cleaning the apartment with two broken legs; there's one more task — cleaning himself
jokes.punchline: He's going to bathe himself using the method his parents use to wash their dog
jokes.explanation: The detail that Andy's parents wash him like a dog because he can't shower is beautifully absurd and deeply character-specific — it's the perfect encapsulation of Andy's helplessness and his family's creative problem-solving. The 'this is how they clean their dog' reveal is the punchline and it lands hard. Strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: Andy has written a song for Ann and it's playing on a boom box when she arrives. 'I wrote that for Ann. It's gonna be playing when she walks through the door today. And check this out. Washed my shorts. How do you like that?'
jokes.setup: Andy has been preparing a grand romantic gesture for Ann's return
jokes.punchline: His triumphant achievement alongside the song is that he washed his shorts — the disproportion between the romantic gesture and the humble domestic one is the joke
jokes.explanation: The 'washed my shorts' as a triumphant parallel achievement to a romantic song is a good character beat. Andy genuinely thinks this is impressive, and that sincerity makes it funny. Very Andy — the bar for success is simply 'I did a thing.'

jokes.text: Andy fights his neighbor Lawrence over the boom box. 'What are you doing in my yard, Lawrence? Get out of here.' / 'I just put 12 new batteries in that thing!'
jokes.setup: Andy has a boom box playing loudly for Ann's arrival; his neighbor Lawrence comes to complain and takes the boom box
jokes.punchline: 'I just put 12 new batteries in that thing!' — Andy's indignation is about the batteries, not the emotional significance of the song
jokes.explanation: 'I just put 12 new batteries in that thing!' is a great line — 12 batteries in a boom box is already funny (why does it need 12?), and the fact that Andy's emotional investment in the boom box fight is purely about the batteries and not the romantic gesture is very Andy. The number 12 is specific enough to be funny on its own.

jokes.text: Ron defends Leslie to the committee: 'This is not communist China. You cannot make her whip herself. You cannot make her wear a hair shirt.' / 'We weren't planning on doing either of those things.'
jokes.setup: Ron is defending Leslie against the disciplinary committee; he escalates his rhetoric dramatically
jokes.punchline: The committee flatly says they weren't planning on making her do any of those things — Ron's defense was against imaginary tyrannies
jokes.explanation: Ron's libertarian escalation to whipping and hair shirts for a gift basket offense is both character-perfect and structurally excellent. The committee's quiet 'we weren't planning on doing either of those things' is a perfect deadpan deflation. Ron fighting against self-flagellation on behalf of someone who has been desperately self-flagellating all episode is a great ironic reversal. Earns 8.

jokes.text: Ron: 'You want to live in North Korea, you can live in North Korea.' / Committee: 'I don't want to. I want to live in America.'
jokes.setup: Ron is making a dramatic anti-government/anti-communist case for Leslie's freedom
jokes.punchline: The committee member, confused, clarifies they don't want to live in North Korea — deflating Ron's grand rhetoric to a literal conversation
jokes.explanation: The literalization of Ron's rhetorical North Korea threat is a great straight-man response. The committee member simply declining to live in North Korea is so earnest and deflating that it perfectly punctures Ron's libertarian grandstanding. Good economy and strong character integration for Ron.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'No, I didn't do it for Leslie. I did it because I hate bureaucracy. My idea of a perfect government is one guy, who sits in a small room at a desk, and the only thing he's allowed to decide is who to nuke.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just defended Leslie heroically in the hearing; he's now explaining his real motivation
jokes.punchline: His perfect government vision is a solitary nuclear decision-maker — the reduction of all government to one guy with a nuclear button
jokes.explanation: This is one of Ron Swanson's definitive character-establishing speeches. The vision of government reduced to one man in a room whose only power is nuclear strikes is perfectly absurd while being completely consistent with Ron's anti-government libertarianism. It's a rich idea compressed into a few lines. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Ron continues: 'The man is chosen based on some kind of IQ test, and maybe also a physical tournament, like a decathlon.'
jokes.setup: Ron has described his ideal government as one person who decides who to nuke
jokes.punchline: The selection process includes a decathlon — athletic excellence is apparently necessary for nuclear authority
jokes.explanation: The addition of 'maybe also a physical tournament, like a decathlon' to the IQ test selection criteria is a great escalation. The 'maybe also' suggests Ron is workshopping this in real time and the decathlon is an afterthought he actually likes. Character-perfect — Ron values physical strength and mental toughness in equal measure. Part of a larger bit that together forms one of the episode's standout sequences.

jokes.text: Leslie confesses to Ann she did it for a guy: 'I did it for a guy.' / 'Oh! Yeah. Mark.'
jokes.setup: Leslie told Ann she opened the basket to 'shatter the glass ceiling' and infiltrate the boys' club
jokes.punchline: The real reason was simpler — she did it for a guy (Mark); Ann immediately knows which guy
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Leslie's feminist framing (she did it for a MAN) is the episode's thematic punchline. Ann's instant 'Oh! Yeah. Mark.' with no hesitation is perfect — she already knew. A good character revelation that also recontextualizes the whole episode. Well-structured misdirection.

jokes.text: Ann's reaction to learning Leslie opened the basket for a guy — specifically Mark: 'Oh. Oh. Wow.'
jokes.setup: Leslie admits she did everything for romantic reasons involving Mark
jokes.punchline: Ann's three-beat reaction — 'Oh. Oh. Wow.' — says everything without saying anything; it's the face of someone reassessing their friend's decision-making
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat — the three-word response says more than an explanation would. Economy is high but it's mostly performance-dependent.

jokes.text: Ann's talking head: 'Smart woman. Iffy choice in men. But then again, I'm not one to talk.' [clearly referencing Andy]
jokes.setup: Ann has just heard that Leslie risked her job for a man
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not one to talk' — Ann, who is caring for her freeloading ex-boyfriend with two broken legs, is in no position to judge romantic choices
jokes.explanation: Ann's self-deprecating acknowledgment is a good line that threads her story through Leslie's. The audience immediately understands the callback to Andy without it being spelled out. 'Smart woman. Iffy choice in men' is a well-constructed two-part observation, and the button 'I'm not one to talk' lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Andy to Ann upon her return: 'Somebody is getting gently laid tonight.'
jokes.setup: Andy has cleaned the house and written Ann a song; he's presenting it all proudly upon her return
jokes.punchline: His confident prediction of sex is undermined by the qualifier 'gently' — a reference to his broken legs limiting mobility
jokes.explanation: The word 'gently' does all the work here — Andy's pride and confidence in announcing sex while having two broken legs is captured in that one qualifier. It's crude but smart: the specificity of 'gently' transforms it from a simple sex joke into a character joke about Andy's physical limitations and his relentless optimism. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Mark offers Leslie a beer on government property: 'You're not supposed to be drinking on government property.' / 'Loosen up. You're gonna drive yourself crazy trying to follow every single rule in government.' / 'Mark, I have a letter in my file.' / 'I got seven letters in my file. Pretty much every guy in city planning has a bunch of letters.'
jokes.setup: After the ordeal of the hearing, Mark offers Leslie a beer to celebrate
jokes.punchline: Mark has SEVEN letters in his file; 'pretty much every guy in city planning has a bunch' — the hearing Leslie agonized over is routine bureaucratic noise for the men
jokes.explanation: This is a smart structural joke that also lands thematically — Leslie's epic self-flagellation and ordeal is literally routine for the men she's trying to equal. The seven letters (vs. her one) provides the scale, and 'pretty much every guy in city planning' generalizes it to institutional indifference. Good observational comedy about gender and institutional standards.

jokes.text: Mark: 'Welcome to the team.' — said while handing Leslie a beer on government property
jokes.setup: Mark has just revealed that having letters in your file is normal for city planners; he hands Leslie a beer on government property — the same thing that got her in trouble
jokes.punchline: 'Welcome to the team.' — the 'team' is people who violate the rules without thinking about it
jokes.explanation: A three-word episode button that pays off the whole theme. 'Welcome to the team' delivered as she accepts a beer on government property is the episode's thesis statement as comedy — the boys' club wasn't a secret society, it's just the everyday act of not following every rule. Clean, economical, earned. Great episode closer.

jokes.text: Mark to Leslie: 'I got seven letters in my file. Pretty much every guy in city planning has a bunch of letters.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is distressed about getting a letter in her file from the disciplinary hearing
jokes.punchline: Mark reveals that letters in file are totally normal — a stack of them, in fact — completely deflating Leslie's sense of disgrace
jokes.explanation: Solid deflation joke. The episode's entire ethical crisis is revealed to be routine for city planning. Mark's casual 'seven letters' is a good character beat and a nice final puncture of Leslie's self-dramatization.

jokes.text: Leslie's final talking head: 'Look out, boys. I'm in your club now. I'm in your club. I'm in your club. I'm in your club. I'm in your club. I'm in your... Mmm. Creepy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been welcomed to 'the team' and is triumphantly claiming her victory for the camera
jokes.punchline: The repetition of 'I'm in your club' escalates until even Leslie notices it's creepy — she self-corrects with 'Mmm. Creepy.'
jokes.explanation: A perfect final beat for the episode. Leslie's triumphant declaration becomes a manic loop that she herself has to interrupt. 'Mmm. Creepy.' as self-acknowledgment is the right button — it shows Leslie's self-awareness just barely outrunning her enthusiasm. The repetition structure builds well and the payoff is sharp. Excellent character integration and a satisfying comedic cap to the episode's theme.

tmdb_overview: Leslie attempts to break into the political "old boy's club," causing an ethical dilemma. Meanwhile, Andy plans a surprise for Ann.
insight: Early Parks finds its rhythm: deadpan character beats sustain an 80-point episode on sparse 1.9 jokes-per-minute density.
